name: The eight consciousnesses

definitions.definition: The five sense-consciousnesses, mental consciousness, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas) and the store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna); the last is the root in which the others arise like waves; the treatises (Triṃśikā, Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Cheng weishi lun) present them as three transformations of consciousness.

The pramāṇa authors (following Dharmakīrti) generally speak only of the six consciousnesses; Tibetan doxography calls them 'Cittamātrins following reasoning' in contrast to 'followers of scripture' who accept eight.

relations.note: Theravāda Abhidhamma counts six consciousnesses with bhavaṅga, no ālaya

notes: U39 contributes the sūtra-layer definition under the same id. The P definition's doxographic claim is the Tibetan tenet-system (grub mtha') account, recorded as such.

definitions.definition: The eighth consciousness: maturation of karma, receptacle of all seeds, appropriator of the body; unperceived, neutral, flowing like a torrent; proved by the need to explain rebirth, the mindless attainments, the continuity of seeds and the simultaneity of cognitions; it ceases as ālaya at arhatship and is transformed at buddhahood into mirror-like wisdom.

relations.note: Faxiang keeps the ālaya distinct from suchness; the Laṅkāvatāra (ch. 6) identifies the tathāgatagarbha with it

definitions.definition: The seventh consciousness, which takes the store-consciousness as its object and thinks 'I', always accompanied by self-view, self-delusion, self-conceit and self-love; it is the source of the sense of 'I' even in unconscious states, and is transformed into the wisdom of equality.

relations.note: its self-grasping is what the knowledge of selflessness removes

definitions.definition: Consciousness transforms as (1) maturation — the store; (2) mentation — the afflicted mind; (3) the apprehension of the six kinds of object; all talk of self and dharmas refers to these.

Five universal, five particular, eleven wholesome, six root afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions and four variable factors, as listed in the Triṃśikā and counted as fifty-one in the Baifa mingmen lun and Cheng weishi lun.

relations.note: the Sarvāstivāda count

definitions.definition: Mental consciousness does not arise among the non-perceiving gods, in the attainments of non-perception and of cessation, in deep dreamless sleep and in fainting; in these the store-consciousness continues.

Experience and action perfume the store-consciousness, leaving seeds that ripen as future consciousness and its objects; the imprints of karma together with those of the twofold grasping produce rebirth; for Dharmapāla seeds are both innate and newly perfumed.
Beginningless imprints of conceptualization make cognition appear as grasped and grasper and make universals seem real.

relations.note: Sautrāntika seeds lie in the mental series itself, without an ālaya

name: The six characteristics of seeds

definitions.definition: Seeds are momentary, simultaneous with their fruit, continuous as a series, determinate in moral quality, dependent on conditions and productive only of their own fruit (Mahāyānasaṃgraha).

notes: Sanskrit names reconstructed from the Chinese/Tibetan; list recalled.

definitions.definition: Each cognition has a seen part (image), a seeing part, a self-witnessing part and a witnessing of the self-witnessing part (Dharmapāla, adopted by Xuanzang); others admitted one (Sthiramati: only self-witnessing is real), two (Nanda) or three (Dignāga) parts.

relations.note: Dignāga's three-aspect cognition is the basis

definitions.definition: The dependent nature as the minds and mental factors of the three realms: it exists, while the duality of grasped and grasper it projects does not; emptiness exists within it.

relations.note: it is the dependent nature

definitions.definition: The three realms are only cognition: objects appearing as external are cognition appearing as objects, as in a dream; this is argued by the Viṃśatikā against objections from proponents of external objects (restriction of place and time, intersubjectivity, efficacy, atoms) and in its final sense is the perfected nature itself, realized when consciousness no longer apprehends an object.
Dharmakīrti argues from the co-apprehension of blue and its cognition that they are not different; cognition, undivided in itself, appears divided into grasped and grasper to deluded vision.

relations.note: the treatise-layer form of the sūtras' 'mind-only'
the atom is refuted as neither one nor many

definitions.definition: Every dharma is understood through the imagined (how it appears: duality, own-being posited by names — non-existent), the dependent (what appears: imagination arising from conditions — existent but not as it appears) and the perfected (the dependent's constant absence of the imagined — suchness); they are neither one nor different; entering them in order, understanding, abandonment and attainment happen at once.

relations.note: Madhyamaka reads the Prajñāpāramitā through two truths; Yogācāra through three natures

definitions.definition: The Prajñāpāramitā's 'all dharmas are without own-nature' was spoken with the three natures in view: the imagined lacks own-characteristic, the dependent lacks self-arising, the perfected is the ultimate naturelessness.

Everything is neither empty nor non-empty: unreal imagination exists, duality does not, emptiness exists in it — avoiding both the extreme of superimposition (that duality exists) and of denial (that nothing exists).

relations.note: Madhyamaka's middle way is the emptiness of all own-being, including of consciousness

definitions.definition: Emptiness is the non-existence of duality and the existence of that non-existence; its synonyms are suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate and the dharmadhātu; it is neither defiled nor pure; the ultimate is neither existent nor non-existent.

relations.note: the Yogācāra 'other-emptiness-like' formula: X is empty of duality, and the emptiness exists
emptiness is the perfected nature

name: The luminous mind (prabhāsvara-citta)

definitions.definition: Mind is luminous by nature and the defilements are adventitious; hence emptiness is neither defiled nor pure; only the mind that is dharmatā is called luminous by nature.
Because mind is luminous by nature and the stains adventitious, the stains can be wholly removed by cultivating their antidote (seeing selflessness).

notes: Shared id (U38 contributes the early-school definition).

definitions.definition: Selflessness of persons (removing the afflictive obscuration) and selflessness of dharmas (removing the cognitive obscuration); the first is entered through the teaching of aggregates and fields, the second through cognition-only.
A cognition that does not construct its object, first attained on the path of seeing; preparatory, fundamental and subsequently-obtained; not absence of thought, sleep or unconsciousness.

At buddhahood the transformed basis is mirror-like wisdom, on which depend the wisdoms of equality, discernment and accomplishment; in the Cheng weishi lun they are the transformed eighth, seventh, sixth and five sense consciousnesses.

relations.note: consciousness-to-wisdom mapping of the Cheng weishi lun

definitions.definition: Liberation and buddhahood as the turning of the basis — the ālaya or the dependent nature — from defiled to purified through the abandonment of the twofold badness; begun at the first ground, completed after the diamond-like concentration; it is the undefiled element, the dharma-body.
The buddhas' nirvāṇa, abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in quiescence, by wisdom and compassion.

name: The three bodies of a buddha (Yogācāra)

definitions.definition: The pure dharmadhātu operates as the natural (essential) body, the enjoyment body and the emanation body, the first being the basis of the other two; the Abhisamayālaṃkāra counts four by distinguishing the wisdom dharmakāya.

relations.note: the systematization of the sūtras' buddha-bodies

name: Phenomena and their nature (dharma and dharmatā)

definitions.definition: All knowables are summed up as dharmas — the appearance of duality and names, saṃsāra — and dharmatā — suchness free of grasped and grasper, nirvāṇa; the transformation of the basis is the shift from the one to the other.

Reality as established by worldly convention, by reasoning, as the domain of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscuration, and as the domain of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscuration — the supreme suchness.
All dharmas are by nature inexpressible; words attach to designations and imagined natures, not to the thing's own nature, which is the object of non-conceptual cognition.
The particular is inexpressible; words and concepts reach only exclusions.

name: Spiritual lineage (gotra) and the five lineages

definitions.definition: Beings have a lineage for awakening either naturally present or developed; they belong to the disciples', solitary buddhas', bodhisattvas' or undetermined lineage, and some to none (agotra); the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra also says all beings have suchness as their embryo. Faxiang (Kuiji) teaches the five fixed lineages.

relations.note: Tathāgatagarbha teaching: all beings will become buddhas

definitions.definition: Rebirth is the store-consciousness's continuation: when a maturation is exhausted, the imprints of karma and of the twofold grasping produce a new one; the ālaya appropriates the new body at conception.

name: Death and dying in Yogācāra

definitions.definition: At death the store-consciousness is the last to leave the body and at conception the first to enter it; the body grows cold progressively — for those of good karma from the lower body upward, for those of bad karma from the head downward — until consciousness leaves at the heart; the intermediate existence follows.

notes: Recalled from the Yogācārabhūmi (manobhūmi) and Xuanzang's Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses (Bashi guiju song: 'last to go, first to come'); refs not located in this pass.

definitions.definition: Mental action is the gravest of the three kinds of action, as the sages' anger emptied the Daṇḍaka forest — which shows that minds act directly on minds without external objects.
Pliancy and workability of mind lead to the higher knowledges and travel to other realms to honour buddhas; yet even knowledge of others' minds does not accord with its object except in a buddha.

name: The five temperaments (carita) and their remedies

definitions.definition: Practitioners dominated by lust, hatred, delusion, conceit or discursive thought are given the unattractive, loving-kindness, dependent origination, the analysis of elements and mindfulness of breathing respectively.

name: The four kinds of meditation object (Śrāvakabhūmi)

definitions.definition: The pervasive object (images with and without conceptualization, the limit of things, the accomplishment of the aim), objects purifying temperament, objects of skill (aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, the possible and impossible) and objects purifying defilements (the coarse and peaceful aspects of the levels; the four truths).

notes: Sub-lists of the object of skill and of purification recalled; the fourfold division checked in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The reality of a meditative object is established by the reasoning of dependence, of efficacy, of valid proof (through perception, inference and scripture) and of the nature of things.

name: The nine stages of settling the mind (Yogācāra sources)

definitions.definition: Placing, settling firmly, re-settling, settling closely, taming, calming, fully calming, one-pointing and concentrating; with six powers (hearing, reflection, mindfulness, awareness, vigour, familiarity) and four attentions (forced, interrupted, uninterrupted, spontaneous); the five faults and eight remedies of the Madhyāntavibhāga are the obstacles and antidotes along the way.

relations.note: calm is a requisite of the path of preparation

name: The seventeen stages of the Yogācārabhūmi

definitions.definition: The basic section's seventeen stages, from the five sense-consciousnesses through the stages of hearing, reflection and cultivation and of the three vehicles to nirvāṇa with and without remainder.

Accumulation, preparation (four aids to penetration), seeing (sixteen moments; first ground), cultivation (remaining grounds) and completion; the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Triṃśikā describe the passage from preparation to seeing as the progressive abandonment of the grasped and the grasper.

Mounting to mind-only, not imagining external objects; resting in suchness and passing beyond mind-only; passing beyond the imageless; abiding in the imageless and seeing the Mahāyāna — read by Kamalaśīla as stages of meditation.

name: The eight topics and seventy points of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra

definitions.definition: Three knowledges (of all aspects, of paths, of bases), four trainings (full realization of all aspects, culmination, serial, instantaneous) and the dharmakāya.

name: The three kinds of bodhisattva discipline

definitions.definition: Discipline of restraint (the prātimokṣa vows), of gathering wholesome dharmas, and of benefiting beings; with the four offences equivalent to defeat.
Generosity, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation, wisdom, skill in means, aspiration, power and knowledge, matched to the ten grounds.

name: The three turnings of the wheel

definitions.definition: The Saṃdhinirmocana classifies the teaching as three turnings, the third — distinguishing the three natures — being definitive.

name: The ten Indian masters of the Cheng weishi lun

definitions.definition: The ten commentators on the Thirty Verses whose views Xuanzang compiled: Dharmapāla, Guṇamati, Sthiramati, Bandhuśrī, Nanda, Śuddhacandra, Citrabhānu, Viśeṣamitra, Jinaputra and Jñānacandra; Dharmapāla's view is adopted.

notes: Sanskrit forms are the conventional back-translations of the Chinese names; list recalled.

name: The transmission of the Maitreya teachings

definitions.definition: Maitreya taught Asaṅga, who taught Vasubandhu (the 'lineage of vast conduct'); in Tibet the teachings came through Sajjana to Ngok Loden Sherab (the explanatory, analytic transmission) and to Tsen Kawoche (the meditative transmission); two texts were, by tradition, rediscovered by Maitrīpa.

name: The receptacle world as shared cognition

definitions.definition: The store-consciousness imperceptibly cognizes the 'place' — the receptacle world — which appears alike to beings of similar karma (as the river of pus to all hungry ghosts); world-systems arise and perish through the shared karmic imprints of beings.

Objects are understood to arise from mental speech; knowing them as mere speech, the meditator rests in mind-only; the path of calm gathers the names of the teachings, insight investigates their meanings.
The bodhisattva masters the inner science, the science of reasons (logic), the science of language, medicine and the crafts — logic to refute opponents and to inspire faith.

name: Testing the teacher's word by valid cognition

definitions.definition: A teacher's word is accepted not out of respect but after examination by perception and inference, as gold is tested; the Buddha himself is shown to be authoritative by proof, and scripture is relied on only for what perception and inference cannot reach and what they do not contradict.
The bodhisattva vow is to be received from a teacher who holds the vow, is learned and capable.

name: Only two means of valid cognition

definitions.definition: Perception and inference only, because there are only two kinds of object — the particular and the universal; testimony, comparison, presumption and non-perception are included in inference or are not means of knowledge.

relations.note: Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's critique

definitions.definition: The particular is momentary, causally efficacious, ultimately real, inexpressible and known by perception; the universal is a conceptual exclusion, conventionally real, known by inference and words.

name: The two truths in the pramāṇa school

definitions.definition: What is capable of causal efficacy is ultimately real; the rest is conventionally real — while, on the higher (cognition-only) level, even the division into grasped and grasper is conventional.

relations.note: Madhyamaka two truths

name: Graded standpoints: external objects and cognition-only

definitions.definition: Dharmakīrti argues at times as though objects were external (causing images in cognition) and at times from the standpoint of cognition-only, where cognition is non-dual; later commentators (and Tibetan doxographers, who call the school 'Sautrāntika' or 'Yogācāra' accordingly) treat these as successive levels.

notes: Named here with the tradition's own vocabulary (bāhyārtha-naya / vijñapti-naya as used by the commentators); the commentators' labels are recalled.

definitions.definition: Non-conceptual, non-erroneous cognition of the particular; four kinds — sensory, mental, reflexive and yogic; self-evidently free of construction.

Cognition born of the culmination of meditation on a real object — vivid and non-conceptual; the example of those who, disturbed by desire or fear, 'see' absent things shows that cultivation produces vividness; only cultivation of the real (the four truths) makes it a means of knowledge.

Every cognition is aware of itself; this self-awareness is a perception and is the result of the means of knowledge; memory of the cognition proves it had two appearances (of itself and of the object).
The self-witnessing part of cognition (Cheng weishi lun); for Sthiramati the only real part.

name: Means and result of cognition are one

definitions.definition: The means of knowledge (cognition's likeness to the object) and its result (understanding the object, or self-awareness) are one cognition, distinguished only figuratively.

name: The definition of a means of valid cognition

definitions.definition: Non-deceptive cognition (Dharmakīrti), the revealer of a previously unknown object; for Dharmottara, what makes one attain the object; hence memory and re-cognition are not means of knowledge.

name: The three characteristics of a valid reason (trairūpya)

definitions.definition: Presence of the reason in the subject, presence only in similar cases, absence from all dissimilar cases.

name: The three kinds of valid reason

definitions.definition: Effect, own-nature and non-perception — the only reasons grounded in a necessary connection.
Pervasion rests on a real relation of causality or identity between reason and property, not on repeated observation.
Nine possible relations of a reason to similar and dissimilar cases, of which two are valid, two contrary and five inconclusive.

name: Exclusion (apoha) as the meaning of words

definitions.definition: Words and concepts do not reach real universals or the particulars; they apply by excluding what is other; Dharmakīrti grounds this in the similar effects of particulars, Ratnakīrti defines the word-meaning as a positive thing qualified by exclusion.

relations.note: denies the reality of the universal (sāmānya) category; see dsp:reality-of-universals

definitions.definition: (1) From destruction: destruction has no cause, so a thing perishes by nature as soon as it arises (Dharmakīrti); (2) from existence: to exist is to be causally efficacious, which an enduring thing could not be either successively or at once (Dharmottara, Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti: yat sat tat kṣaṇikam).
Blue and the cognition of blue are necessarily apprehended together; hence they are not different; their difference is an error like the double moon.
Cognition in itself is undivided; the division into grasped, grasper and awareness is seen by deluded vision.
Where there is nothing grasped there is no grasping; consciousness abides in cognition-only.

name: The Buddha as a person of valid cognition

definitions.definition: The Buddha has become (bhūta) a means of valid cognition: he knows what is to be abandoned and adopted with its means, through compassion cultivated over many lives and the seeing of selflessness; he is the teacher, the Sugata and the protector; his authority is proved, not assumed.

Breath, senses and cognition do not arise from the body alone without a prior moment of their own kind; so the first moment of mind in a new life comes from a previous mind, and cultivation can continue across lives.

relations.note: consciousness does not arise from the elements of the body alone

definitions.definition: Dharmakīrti infers other minds from observed action and speech, valid for proponents of external objects and of cognition-only alike; Ratnakīrti holds that at the ultimate level they are not established.
Minds influence one another directly as dominant conditions (Viṃśatikā).
Debate aims at truth; only two grounds of defeat are valid; stating superfluous members or using tricks is itself a fault.
Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra and Mādhyamika as a graded sequence (Mokṣākaragupta; later Tibetan grub mtha').
Late Yogācāra divides over whether cognition's images are real (satyākāra: Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti) or false (alīkākāra: Ratnākaraśānti), and whether buddha-cognition has images.
The object-condition must both cause and appear in cognition; atoms cause but do not appear, aggregates appear but do not cause; so the object is the knowable form within cognition.
